text: Before writing a single CREATE TABLE statement, this lesson lays out Driftwood Media's full architecture and the resource-naming convention every later lesson follows -- exactly like a real project's architecture review, before any code gets written.

Billing and product-usage events land daily in a Snowflake internal stage, get copied into raw tables, then dbt transforms them through staging, intermediate, and marts models. An Airflow DAG orchestrates that whole sequence daily, and Power BI's own scheduled refresh picks up the result afterward.

The platform uses two separate virtual warehouses, deliberately. DRIFTWOOD_ETL_WH runs the dbt transformations Airflow triggers -- a workload that spikes during the daily run, then sits idle, so auto-suspend matters. DRIFTWOOD_BI_WH serves Power BI's refresh and ad hoc analyst queries, so reporting never queues behind a dbt run, and its cost shows up separately on the bill.

Every resource shares a driftwood prefix: the DRIFTWOOD_ANALYTICS database, its raw and marts schemas, the driftwood_raw_stage, the two warehouses, and three roles -- transformer, analyst, and compliance. The point isn't the word driftwood itself, it's that every object in a shared account is identifiable as part of this project at a glance.
Next lesson: ingesting data into Snowflake -- the real stage, file format, and COPY INTO pattern that gets billing and usage events landing reliably every day.
